article.overview: A soil friction analyser, as this catalogue uses the term, is an instrument that measures the frictional and shear-strength properties of lunar regolith, mainly its internal friction angle and cohesion. These parameters control how the soil resists sliding, supports loads and yields to digging. The catalogue entry is a functional class label rather than the name of one flown instrument, and no flown lunar instrument carrying this exact name was identified in the sources reviewed. The sources reviewed instead describe related devices: the Apollo 16 self-recording penetrometer, the Soviet Lunokhod cone-vane penetrometer, a laboratory in-situ direct-shear device, and the planned Chang'e 8 Terrain Testing Instrument [1][2][3][4][5].
article.description: Lunar regolith is the loose, fragmented layer that covers the Moon's surface. Its strength is not one fixed value. It depends on grain shape, particle size, density, the stress applied to it and the way it was compacted. Soil engineers describe the shear strength of a granular material with the Coulomb relationship, in which shear strength is the sum of a cohesive term and a frictional term that rises with the normal stress and with the tangent of the friction angle. A soil friction analyser measures these parameters in place. It does so either by moving a shearing device against the soil, or by pushing a cone, blade or vane into it and interpreting the resistance. Rahmatian and Metzger describe lunar simulants as low-cohesion, frictional soils, which makes friction angle a central quantity for lunar surface mechanics [1]. Measurements should therefore record the density and confining stress at which they were made, because the derived friction angle depends on both.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Friction and strength parameters inform several engineering and science questions. They govern the stability of slopes and crater walls, the bearing capacity beneath landers, rovers and future structures, the traction and sinkage of wheels, and the forces needed for excavation and sampling. Rahmatian and Metzger conclude that a modified shear vane tester may be useful for surface use by astronauts or a robotic lander, because it could extract several key soil parameters [1]. Penetration and cone-vane data from Apollo and Lunokhod also constrain how the strength of the regolith changes with depth [4][5]. A soil friction analyser therefore serves engineering design and geotechnical characterisation rather than a single geophysical observation.
article.operating_principle: Three measurement approaches appear in the sources reviewed. The first is penetration. A cone is pushed into the regolith and the resistance is recorded against depth. The Apollo 16 self-recording penetrometer used this method and recorded penetration resistance on a drum in its upper housing, with a lunar-surface reference plane defining the depth datum [4]. Soil strength was then inferred using a failure model, which the source describes as a wedge-failure model that closely matches dense, fine, sandy soils [4]. The second is cone-vane testing. A cone is pushed in, and a shear vane is then rotated to measure shear resistance as a function of shear angle. The Chang'e 8 Terrain Testing Instrument combines this approach with a cone penetrometer [3]. The third is direct shear. A laboratory device described by Jerves and colleagues uses a box nested inside a larger open-bottomed box. Two rotating plates clear the surrounding material so that the inner box can shear without that soil's resistance, and the friction angle and cohesion are then inferred from the test [2]. The Chang'e 8 instrument also uses a permittivity sensor, with electrodes integrated into the shear vanes, to infer bulk density and ice content from the regolith's dielectric properties [3].
article.scientific_importance: Remote sensing and orbital imagery show the lunar surface but cannot directly measure how regolith will bear a load or resist sliding. In-situ strength measurements therefore supply information that cannot be obtained from above. The Apollo 16 analysis shows the limits of penetration data: one measurement does not give a unique pair of cohesion and friction angle, and unique values need two cone sizes in the same soil or resistance at two depths in a homogeneous deposit [4]. Rahmatian and Metzger found that none of the field geotechnical instruments they tested was adequate for a low-cohesion, frictional soil, although a modified shear vane tester could extract several important parameters [1]. A modern instrument must therefore be designed around low cohesion and high friction, and should be able to resolve parameters that a single penetration test cannot separate.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a soil friction analyser. The catalogue class can include penetrometers, cone-vane testers, direct-shear devices and combinations of these. The examples below describe named instruments only, and their values must not be transferred to other designs.

examples.name: Apollo 16 Self-Recording Penetrometer (SRP)
examples.status: Flown on the lunar surface during Apollo 16 (documented in the Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report)
examples.measurement: Penetration resistance recorded as a function of depth below the surface on a drum in the upper housing.
examples.limitations_stated: A single penetration record does not give a unique cohesion and friction angle pair; the friction ratio was assumed from simulant friction tests.
examples.description: The Apollo 16 self-recording penetrometer pushed a cone into the lunar surface and recorded the resistance against depth. The cones have a 30 degree apex angle and two base areas of 1.29 cm2 and 3.22 cm2. A bearing plate measuring 2.54 by 12.7 cm defines the bearing footprint. The reported maximum penetration depth is 76 cm and the maximum recordable penetration force is 215 N [4]. The source does not report the instrument mass or the shaft dimensions. Soil-strength parameters were deduced with a wedge-failure model, and the friction ratio delta over phi was set to 0.5, based on friction tests between a ground basalt lunar soil simulant and hard anodised aluminium [4]. The source states that penetration data alone do not give a unique solution for cohesion and friction angle [4].
examples.notes: No images verified for this example. The deployment method is not reported in the source read.

examples.name: Lunokhod cone-vane penetrometer (PROP)
examples.type: Historical lunar rover instrument (Soviet Lunokhod 1 and 2)
examples.status: Flown on Lunokhod rovers, per the sources reviewed; the 1972 NASA technical report was reviewed only through a search extract
examples.description: The Lunokhod cone-vane penetrometer, also written PROP or PrOP in some sources, combined a cone and a vane on a rover. A 1972 NASA technical report on the Lunokhod-1 penetrometer gives a cone base of 5.0 cm, a cone height of 4.4 cm, a 60 degree cone angle and a vane diameter of 7.0 cm [5]. These values were obtained from a search extract of that report and have not been checked against the full scanned text. The source extract does not report the mass. The cone-vane device was used to estimate bearing capacity, and it did not measure all soil strength properties [5].
examples.notes: Geometry is from a search extract, not from a full read. Treat as unverified until checked against the scanned report.

examples.name: In-situ direct-shear and sinkage device (Caltech)
examples.status: Laboratory device; no flight, and the abstract does not report field deployment
examples.measurement: Coulomb cohesion and internal friction angle inferred from a direct-shear test; Bekker parameters said to be inferable but not reported.
examples.description: The device described by Jerves and colleagues uses a box nested inside a larger open-bottomed box. Two rotating plates clear the surrounding material so that the inner box can shear without that material's resistance. The abstract states that the test allows Coulomb parameters, including cohesion and internal friction angle, to be inferred, and that Bekker parameters can also be inferred [2]. The abstract describes a laboratory device that could be placed on the underside of a rover. It does not report numerical measurements, dimensions, mass or a rover-wheel variant [2].
examples.notes: The full PDF was not readable through the fetch tool. The description relies on the repository abstract.

examples.name: Chang'e 8 Terrain Testing Instrument (TTI)
examples.status: Planned for the Chang'e 8 mission, with launch slated for 2029. The structural model has been delivered; the electrical model is planned for summer 2026. No flight hardware is reported.
examples.mass_note: Approximate total TTI mass of about 1.5 kg, including an electronics unit housed inside the rover.
examples.depth_note: Approximate depth range of about 5 cm.
sensors: permittivity sensor (electrodes integrated into the shear vanes)
examples.carrier: JINNAH-1 rover, with a contribution from SUPARCO
examples.measurement: Penetration resistance from the cone; shear resistance as a function of shear angle from the rotating front vane; bulk density and ice content inferred from permittivity.
examples.description: The Terrain Testing Instrument is a vane-cone instrument. A linear translation mechanism presses the vane-cone assembly into the regolith, the cone measures penetration resistance, and the front shear vane rotates to indicate shear resistance as a function of shear angle. Electrodes integrated into the shear vanes form a permittivity sensor that is intended to infer bulk density and ice content [3]. The instrument is carried on the JINNAH-1 rover, with a contribution from SUPARCO, for China's Chang'e 8 lunar landing and roving mission. The abstract reports multiple measurement sequences at various locations during the first lunar day after landing, but it does not report the number of sequences, measured values, accuracy or resolution [3]. The abstract indicates that the structural model has been delivered and vibration tested on a rover structural model, and that an electrical model follows [3].
examples.notes: Planned instrument. The abstract is preliminary and gives no performance specifications.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Apollo 16 SRP: cone base areas 1.29 cm2 and 3.22 cm2; bearing plate 2.54 by 12.7 cm; shaft dimensions not reported [4]. Lunokhod PROP: cone base 5.0 cm, cone height 4.4 cm, vane diameter 7.0 cm, from a search extract of [5]. TTI: depth range about 5 cm [3]. Caltech device: no dimensions reported [2]. The designs differ, so these values are not directly comparable.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Apollo 16 SRP and Lunokhod PROP: mass not reported. Caltech device: not reported. TTI: approximately 1.5 kg total including an electronics unit housed inside the rover [3]. The approximate TTI mass should not be compared with the other examples, whose masses are not reported.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not reported for any example in the sources read.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A soil friction analyser must work in the lunar surface environment, which has no substantial atmosphere, large temperature variations between lunar day and night, abrasive fine dust and exposure to radiation. Its electronics and mechanisms need thermal protection, and its mechanical actuation must work reliably in dust. The surface support also needs to be stable, because the measurement depends on a known reaction force. Laboratory validation adds its own requirements. Rahmatian and Metzger tested three lunar simulants, JSC-1A, NU-LHT-2M and CHENOBI, compacted by vibration under overburden. They also found that JSC-1A does not behave mechanically like the other simulants, probably because its particles are more rounded, and that a natural lunar analog soil, BP-1, behaves much like NU-LHT-2M and CHENOBI [1]. Simulant choice and test preparation therefore strongly affect what a laboratory result means for the Moon.
article.limitations: A soil friction analyser gives parameters that depend on a model and on assumptions. Penetration data alone do not determine cohesion and friction angle uniquely, and the Apollo 16 analysis depends on an assumed friction ratio [4]. Direct-shear and vane devices give different quantities, so results from different instrument types should not be compared without a common interpretation. The Caltech device is a laboratory prototype whose abstract reports no measured values [2]. The Chang'e 8 TTI penetrates only about 5 cm into the regolith, which limits what it can say about deeper layers [3]. No instrument reviewed reported a measured lunar friction angle from flight data in the sources read. Simulant results may not transfer to the Moon, and no source reviewed claims an accuracy figure for a flown friction measurement.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A soil friction analyser can be delivered to the Moon as part of a rover, as a lander payload with its own deployment mechanism, or as an astronaut-deployed experiment. The examples reviewed show each route. The Chang'e 8 TTI is carried on a rover, with its electronics unit inside the rover [3]. The Caltech device abstract only says it could be placed on the underside of a rover [2]. The Apollo 16 penetrometer was part of the lunar surface experiment package, and the source read does not report its deployment method [4].
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument with a lander or rover on Earth, including its mechanical mounts and electrical harness.
Launch the spacecraft on a launch vehicle and transfer it towards the Moon.
Land the lander or rover on the lunar surface.
Deploy the instrument, or for a rover-mounted instrument, operate it through the rover's mechanisms; the TTI uses a linear translation mechanism to press the vane-cone assembly into the regolith [3].
Connect power and data interfaces and record measurement sequences; the TTI abstract refers to sequences during the first lunar day [3].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Deployment methods reviewed include penetration by a linear mechanism on a rover (TTI) [3], a nested-box device that shears the soil in situ (Caltech) [2], and a penetrometer used during the Apollo 16 surface experiments, for which the source read does not report the deployment method [4]. A future instrument would need to define how its reaction force is provided, because penetration and shear tests need a stable reaction on the surface.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 16 self-recording penetrometer and the Lunokhod cone-vane penetrometer are the two historical lunar examples reviewed [4][5]. The Terrain Testing Instrument is a planned example that combines a cone and a vane with a permittivity sensor [3].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: A future soil friction analyser's compatibility with a particular lander or rover has not been assessed. Mass, mounting points, reaction loads and power and data interfaces would need to be compared with verified spacecraft specifications before any compatibility claim is made. The TTI's approximate mass of 1.5 kg and the rover carrier are reported in the abstract, but no lander interface data were found [3].

article.historical_significance: The Apollo penetrometers and the Lunokhod cone-vane instrument were among the early in-situ measurements of lunar soil strength. The Apollo 16 analysis shows that these measurements gave useful but non-unique estimates [4]. Rahmatian and Metzger's laboratory evaluation showed that the field geotechnical tools available at the time were not adequate for low-cohesion, frictional soil, which shaped the case for a modified shear vane [1]. The planned Chang'e 8 TTI continues this line of work and adds permittivity-based density and ice sensing [3].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The payload name 'soil friction analyser' describes a class of measurements rather than one standard instrument. The Apollo, Lunokhod, Caltech and Chang'e 8 examples are not interchangeable. Values such as mass, dimensions, depth and measured strength must always be tied to a named instrument and source. Evidence gaps include: the Caltech PDF could not be read through the fetch tool; the Lunokhod geometry comes from a search extract; the TTI evidence is a preliminary conference abstract; EGU25-14967, an earlier TTI abstract, was withdrawn and was not used for data; and no commercial or flown instrument named 'soil friction analyser' was identified.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL query strings and fragments removed. No image URLs were verified, so no image objects are included; all arrays are empty.

data_quality_notes: The catalogue name 'Soil friction analyser' is a functional class label. No flown or named instrument with this exact name was identified.

Apollo 16 SRP values (30 degree apex angle, cone base areas, bearing plate, 76 cm maximum depth, 215 N maximum force, friction ratio 0.5) are from the Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report read in full.

Lunokhod PROP geometry (5.0 cm base, 4.4 cm height, 60 degree cone angle, 7.0 cm vane) comes from a search extract of a 1972 NASA technical report; the scanned PDF could not be read and the values are unverified.
The Caltech in-situ direct-shear device is described from its repository abstract only; the PDF was not readable, and no measured values or flight status are reported.

The Chang'e 8 TTI evidence is a preliminary EPSC 2026 abstract. The structural model is delivered, the electrical model is planned, and no performance data were published. Its mass (about 1.5 kg) and depth (about 5 cm) are approximate values from the abstract.
EGU25-14967, an earlier TTI abstract, was withdrawn and was not used for data.
No image URLs were verified from official pages, so the article contains no image objects. Image research was not completed.
Search quota: six WebSearch calls and ten WebFetch calls were used. Two fetches of the Apollo 16 soil mechanics chapter and the Lunokhod report failed (404 and binary/scanned content respectively).
